newsitem.title: USA: NAPM report shows stronger manufacturing in August.
newsitem.headline: NAPM report shows stronger manufacturing in August.

text.p: The National Association of Purchasing Management said on Tuesday its index of manufacturing activity rose last month, although many executives described August as "flat."
"Purchasing executives' comments on business conditions in August generally indicated little or no change from July," the NAPM said in a statement.
The group's monthly index climbed to 52.6 last month from 50.2 in July.
The report somewhat calmed investor fears that the economy was still growing rapidly and Wall Street stocks and the inflation-sensitive 30-year U.S. Treasury bond rebounded from early lows.

In another report issued Tuesday, the Conference Board said the Index of Leading Indicators, which is supposed to forecast economic trends six to nine months ahead, rose by 0.2 percent after a 0.5 percent increase in June.

It was a sixth consecutive monthly increase in the broad-based gauge of national activity and fit with other recent reports showing the economy was slowing only gradually after the strongest second-quarter expansion in two years.

The Purchasing Managers' Index, at 52.6 percent for August, was the second-highest reading since 56.3 in January 1995, with only June 1996 and February 1995, both at 54.3, exceeding the August number.
A reading above 50 indicates that the manufacturing economy is generally expanding, while a reading below 50 indicates that activity is generally contracting.
August was only the fourth month since July 1995 that the PMI has indicated manufacturing growth.
However, Ralph Kauffman, chairman of NAPM's business survey committee, told reporters that most purchasing managers saw little price pressure and no real shortage in labour.
"It appears that things are probably going to stay relatively calm in the price sector," Kauffman said. "There were very few comments dealing with the experiences of increased prices."
He noted that NAPM members have indicated over the past few months that they expect U.S. economic conditions to gradually get better.
"They generally think things are going to continue to improve at a slow and steady rate," he said.
Kauffman also said he did not foresee "any tremendous or large increases in production" over the near term.
The survey of purchasing executives across the country showed that production, new orders, and new export orders all grew at faster rates last month than in July.
It also indicated that inventories, employment, and prices decreased at slower rates in August, although order backlogs and supplier delivery performance decreased more rapidly.
The NAPM said manufacturing employment decreased in August for the 19th consecutive month, although the rate of decrease slowed somewhat from July.

"Aside from the comments of a few members that they are experiencing some problems ... there just doesn't seem to be any real shortage of employment prospects to meet the current demand of employment in manufacturing," Kauffman said.

The employment index for August rose by 2.7 points to 48.2 from 45.5 in July. An employment index below 47, over time, is generally consistent with contraction in the Bureau of Labour Statistics data on manufacturing employment.
The NAPM's August price index of 47.4 marked the third consecutive month of lower prices, although prices declined at a slower rate than in July, when the index was 44.5.
In August, 20 percent of purchasing executives reported paying lower prices, compared with 24 percent who indicated lower prices in July.
The monthly NAPM report is based on data compiled from replies to questions asked of purchasing executives in more than 300 industrial companies.
